hints.S50_A1: He CATCHES THE FEATHERED SHUTTLECOCK BEFORE IT TOUCHED THE GROUND, and he is compared to a CAT. Ask: which word matches a cat's speed of reaction? 'Slow', 'clumsy' and 'heavy' all describe someone who would drop it.
hints.S50_A2: He KEPT TRYING UNTIL THE VERY END even after LOSING FIVE ROUNDS IN A ROW, and REFUSED flips the meaning of the blank. Ask: which phrasal verb means to stop trying because something feels too hard?
hints.S50_A3: It is only A TINY SPECK AGAINST THE BLUE SKY now that it has flown HIGHER AND HIGHER. Ask: which word means able to be seen at all? 'Colourful' talks about colour, and rising does not make a kite heavy or broken.
hints.S50_A4: The top must end up SPINNING PERFECTLY ON THE GROUND, so it has to be thrown and released with force. Ask: which verb means to set something moving with a strong, controlled release? 'Break' and 'sell' have nothing to do with spinning.
hints.S50_A5: The dash spells it out: BOTH HANDS AND EYES MUST WORK TOGETHER AT EXACTLY THE RIGHT MOMENT. Ask: which noun names that teamwork between body parts? 'Strength' is raw power, and 'speed' alone will not catch the stones.
hints.S50_B1: Do not be fooled by THE PLAYGROUND full of children: the subject is EVERYONE, which counts as ONE. Ask: in the present tense, which ending does a singular subject put on its verb? 'Are playing' and 'have played' both treat it as plural.
hints.S50_B2: HAS is waiting for a past participle, and SINCE IT WAS FOUNDED stretches from the past to today. Ask: is 'hold' a regular verb that takes -ed, or an irregular one that changes its vowel? 'Has hold' and 'has holding' are impossible.
hints.S50_B3: LONGER is already a comparative - it ends in -er - so the blank must strengthen it, not repeat it. Ask: can 'very', 'too' or 'most' ever stand in front of a comparative? Only one small word can do that job.
hints.S50_B4: A STRONG GUST OF WIND SUDDENLY SNAPPED THE STRING - there is the interruption. Ask: at that instant, had the children finished, or was the action still going on? Pick the past form that shows an action in mid-flow.
hints.S50_B5: SPACE cannot be counted - you cannot say one space, two spaces, on a MAT. Ask: which option belongs with an uncountable noun? 'Few', 'many' and 'a few' all need things you can count, such as players.
hints.S50_B6: The statement is positive and its verb is ARE. Ask: after a positive statement, which way does the tag turn? The tag must repeat the same verb, so the singular forms 'is' and 'isn't' cannot match GAMES.
hints.S50_B7: The word BY names the doer: THE STUDENTS. A ROPE cannot check its own length. Ask: which choice puts the receiver in the subject position and sets the action in past time? Two options are active, and one is present.
hints.S50_B8: The TILED CORRIDOR is TOO SLIPPERY, so this is a reported prohibition. Ask: after 'told + person', which pattern does the verb take - plain, -ing, -ed, or 'to' + verb? Then place the negative word correctly inside it.
hints.S50_C1: THE SHADE is a patch you stand inside, wrapped around by it, not a point you touch. Ask: which box word suits a space that surrounds you? 'At the shade' is never English, so a point word cannot work.
hints.S50_C2: The key word is SURFACE: the top rests against the SMOOTH CONCRETE and touches it from above. Ask: which box word shows contact with a flat surface? A word for enclosed spaces would put the top underneath the concrete.
hints.S50_C3: A CORNER is a single exact point, not a room to stand inside. Ask: which box word marks a precise meeting point? The word for enclosed spaces is needed elsewhere, and you cannot meet 'under' a corner.
hints.S50_C4: A KITE flies high above things, and it crossed THE TALLEST TREE without touching it. Ask: which box word means above and across the top of something? 'Through' would send the kite straight into the branches.
hints.S50_C5: Priya HID the bag so that NOBODY WOULD TAKE IT - the safest spot is beneath the seat of the BENCH. Ask: which box word means below something? 'Behind' would put the bag at the back, still in plain sight.
hints.S50_C6: The rope enters THE NARROW GAP at one side and comes out at the other, BETWEEN THE TWO PILLARS. Ask: which box word shows passage from one end of an opening to the other? 'Over' would carry the rope above the gap.
hints.S50_C7: HE RAN - he was outside, and then he arrived inside THE COURTYARD. Ask: which box word shows the DIRECTION of a movement rather than a still position? The plain word for enclosed spaces would mean he was already there.
hints.S50_C8: The SLOWEST PLAYER is sent to the back to WAIT FOR THE NEXT ROUND. Ask: which box word means at the rear of something? A line drawn on the ground has nothing beneath it, so 'under' is impossible.
hints.S50_D1: The clue comes after the dash: PLAYED THEM FOR GENERATIONS, and they CONNECT US TO OUR ROOTS. Ask: which box word names the customs handed down from our grandparents? A 'medal' is won, not inherited.
hints.S50_D2: The blank describes GAMES that have come down through the GENERATIONS. Ask: which box word is an adjective meaning long-established and passed down? 'Clumsy' would describe a player, not a whole custom.
hints.S50_D3: The rope is HELD BY somebody, and it is not the jumper - a game needs two sides. Ask: which box word names the person playing against you? The blank follows 'the', so it must be a noun.
hints.S50_D4: The dash defines it exactly: THE ABILITY TO MOVE QUICKLY AND CHANGE DIRECTION WITHOUT LOSING BALANCE. Ask: which box word names that nimbleness? It follows 'a player's', so it must be a noun.
hints.S50_D5: The round has ended, so the SMALL CLOTH BAGS are lying about and must be picked up before THE NEXT THROW. Ask: which box word is a verb meaning to fetch something back? 'Forfeit' would mean giving them away.
hints.S50_E1: Count them: THE PLAYERS LINED UP AT THE STARTING ZONE are many, and each holds a top. Ask: does a plural subject take a singular past verb? The verb must agree with its subject, however far away that subject sits.
hints.S50_E2: The TOPS belong to the players who GRIPPED them. Ask: is the underlined word pointing at a place over there, or showing ownership? Both spellings sound the same, so let the meaning of the sentence decide.
hints.S50_E3: The letter in front of the two vowels is H, not C, so the ordinary rhyme applies. Ask: does 'ACHEIVE' put I before E, or E before I? Swap the pair, then compare with believe, relieve and grieve.
hints.S50_E4: WRAPPED tells you what the teacher did; the underlined word tells you HOW it was done. Ask: which word class modifies a verb - the adjective, or the adverb with its -ly ending? Adjectives belong to nouns, and no noun follows.
hints.S50_E5: The FINAL SCORES belong to the WINNERS - more than one of them. Ask: for a plural owner that already ends in -s, does anything come after the apostrophe? Compare the singular form, where an s does follow it.
hints.S50_F1: IF opens the condition - the thing you must do first. Ask: which of the two facts is the condition, and which is the promised outcome? A condition clause keeps a present verb; 'will' belongs only in the other half.
hints.S50_F2: THE GASING COMPETITION is named in both facts, so it should appear only once. Ask: which fact is the main statement, and which becomes the extra clause fenced off by two commas? The relative pronoun already stands for it.
